studentTask.text: Today's focus: participial, absolute, and other phrase types. Essential question: How does close, evidence-governed attention to participial, absolute, and other phrase types change what a reader or writer is entitled to claim? By the end of this lesson you should be able to: Explain what participial, absolute, and other phrase types means and name the textual signal that tells you it is in play. You'll need: course notebook or digital equivalent; the unit's assigned texts, in an accessible reading representation; citation reference or style manual appropriate to the course.

guidedSupport.text:
Work through this with a facilitator, tutor, or on your own if you're ready:
- Error review: Review the specific errors the learner made about today's lesson. Describe the pattern neutrally. Do not infer effort, motivation, or character from an error.
- Reteach the smallest gap: Re-teach only the smallest prerequisite the errors point to, using a different representation than the first time.
- Varied practice: Three short items on today's lesson in deliberately different forms, so the learner cannot pattern-match a single surface.
- Fresh check: One new item on today's lesson with no support, to test whether the reteach took.

If you get stuck:
- If prerequisite gap: Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for today's lesson, re-teach it on a short passage, then retry one fresh item. Do not write the learner's response.
- If repeated error pattern: Describe the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a correct case, and schedule a short later review of today's lesson.
- If procedure without understanding: Ask the learner to explain why the move for today's lesson works on this text before continuing. Accept explanation in any modality.

independentEvidenceTask.text: Re-attempt today's lesson after targeted reteaching, in three varied forms plus one unsupported check. When finished: Explain what you were doing wrong about today's lesson before, and what you are doing differently now.
